title: Comic Book Flip
aka: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
story: A collector's shop puts a new price on a rare comic every morning. You wrote the prices down over the past few weeks. Looking back, you wonder: if you had bought one copy on some day and sold it to another collector for that day's shop price on a later day, what is the most you could have made?
You must buy before you sell, and you can only do it once. If every possible deal loses money, you would simply not have bought.
task: Write bestFlip(prices). prices[i] is the price on day i. Return the largest value of prices[sell] - prices[buy] over all pairs of days with buy < sell.
If no pair makes a profit, or there are fewer than two days, return 0.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 1 at 22 and sell on day 2 at 41 for a profit of 19. Buying at the lowest price, 18 on day 3, only gets you 35 - 18 = 17. The cheapest day is not always the best day to buy.
The price only falls. Every deal would lose money, so you do not trade and the answer is 0.
The highest price is 40 and the lowest is 5, but 5 comes after 40, so you cannot buy at 5 and sell at 40. The best real deal is 40 - 12 = 28.

hints: Pretend you sell on day 4 in the first example, at 35. Which earlier day would you have wanted to buy on, and why?
For any selling day, the best buying day is simply the cheapest day before it. So the only thing you need from the past is one number.
Walk the days in order and keep the lowest price seen so far. What is the best profit if you sell today?
Keep cheapest (lowest price so far) and best (best profit so far, starting at 0). For each price, first update best with price - cheapest, then update cheapest with price.
bruteForce: Try every buying day with every later selling day and keep the largest difference.

That is about n²/2 pairs. With 100,000 days it is roughly 5 billion pairs. Each selling day rescans all the earlier days to find the cheapest one, even though that answer only changes by one day at a time.

js: * @param {number[]} prices  price on each day, in order
* @return {number} the best profit from one buy then one later sell, or 0

tests.note: rising: buy first day, sell last day
global minimum comes too late to help
new minimum later gives the best deal

js: let cheapest = Infinity; // lowest price on any earlier day
let best = 0;            // not trading is always allowed
best = Math.max(best, price - cheapest); // sell today
cheapest = Math.min(cheapest, price);    // or remember today as a buy
py: cheapest = float("inf")  # lowest price on any earlier day
best = 0                 # not trading is always allowed
best = max(best, price - cheapest)  # sell today
cheapest = min(cheapest, price)     # or remember today as a buy
walkthrough: Flip the question around. Instead of "which pair of days?", ask for each day: "if I sell today, what is my best profit?" The answer is today's price minus the cheapest price before today. Keep that cheapest price as you go, and each day costs one step.
• Day 0, 30: nothing to buy from yet. cheapest = 30, best = 0.
Update best before cheapest. The other way round lets you buy and sell on the same day, which is harmless here (profit 0) but is a bug in problems where it is not.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, with constant work per day.
solution.spaceWhy: Two numbers, however many days there are.
solution.takeaway: When the best pair is "something earlier, then something later", walk once and carry a summary of the past (here the running minimum). Each element then only has to be compared with that summary instead of with every earlier element.
